posts.title: Race breakdown: Los Angeles Marathon (single image)
posts.caption:
Los Angeles Marathon is on Mar 7, 2027, and heat is the variable to watch: in 2026 it hit 82°F (27.8°C) by noon, and close to 1,000 runners stopped at mile 18.

The typical high is a mild 70°F (21.1°C), which is why a warm year catches people out. With 778 ft (237 m) of gain and 1,001 ft (305 m) of loss over 26.2 mi (42.195 km), the course itself is kind. A late-morning heat spike on legs that never trained warm is not. Race day is 16 weeks out.

When to start, counted back from Mar 7:

✅ Gut: race fuel in long runs starting between Dec 13 and Jan 10, race-level carbs by Jan 24 to Feb 7
✅ Pacing: goal-pace work in long runs from Dec 27
✅ Heat: for cover in a warm year, sessions Jan 24 to Feb 21, then 1 to 2 short sessions a week to race day
✅ Taper: the final 2 to 3 weeks, from Feb 14 or Feb 21

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions.

Full breakdown: raceproof.ai/races/los-angeles-marathon (link in bio).

SOURCES: Race numbers and 2026 weather: Raceproof's Los Angeles Marathon race page. Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows. Taper length: Raceproof coach consensus (coaching practice) and Smyth & Lawlor 2021.

posts.title: Research: Downhill repeats and squat strength (Martinez-Navarro et al. 2026, Sports)
posts.caption:
After a 3.1 mi (5 km) downhill run, trail runners who did weekly downhill repeats kept their squat strength (+4%). The rest lost 9.1%.

Martinez-Navarro and colleagues tested 36 experienced trail runners (25 men, 11 women) 4 to 6 weeks before a 65.9 mi (106 km) ultra-trail, with a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent at a 15% grade. The downhill-repeat group also had lower CK, a muscle damage marker (182 vs 290 U/L). Lower bounce and shorter steps on the way down were linked to keeping more strength.

Limits: an exploratory, observational study, so these are links, not proof. Only 21.6% of the runners did downhill repeats, the groups were small, and some did both downhill and strength work. The link between damage after the lab descent and after the race (r = 0.64, 27 finishers) fell to r = 0.429 without two extreme values.

Our take, not a finding of the study: train the descents your race has. Let long runs carry your race's descent per mile, add weekly descent by 10% or less, and make your last big downhill session 10 to 14 days out. That ramp and timing come from coaches, not studies. New to steep downhills? Start with relaxed downhills inside your long runs, and if soreness lasts more than about 3 days, wait for it to clear before the next one.

How often do you run downhill on purpose?

Save this for your next build.

SOURCES: Martinez-Navarro et al. 2026, Downhill Running-Induced Muscle Damage in Trail Runners: An Exploratory Study Regarding Training Background and Running Gait, Sports 14(1), doi.org/10.3390/sports14010012. Ramp: Raceproof adaptation rates (coaching practice: Uphill Athlete, Stewart via TrainingPeaks). Timing: Raceproof adaptation windows.

#raceproof #trailrunning #ultrarunning #downhillrunning #hillrunning

What they found: squat strength after the descent, +4% with weekly downhill repeats vs minus 9.1% for the rest. CK, a muscle damage marker, 182 vs 290 U/L, lower with downhill repeats. 21.6% of the runners did weekly downhill repeats, so that group was small.

The key finding, bar chart of squat strength change after a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent: weekly downhill repeats +4%, no downhill repeats minus 9.1%. Average change, +4 plus or minus 10% vs minus 9.1 plus or minus 16.8%, d = 0.87. A link, not proof. Runners chose their own training, and some also lifted.

The study: 36 experienced trail runners, 25 men and 11 women, entered in a 65.9 mi (106 km) ultra-trail. Test: a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent at a 15% grade, 4 to 6 weeks before the race. Exploratory lab and field study. Observational, small groups.

What the study points to: 1, weekly downhill repeats were linked to legs that held up better on a long descent. 2, lower bounce and shorter steps on the way down were linked to keeping more strength. Summary from the Raceproof research library, not the authors' words.

Our take, not a finding of the study: train the descents your race has. Long runs carry your race's descent per mile. Add weekly descent by 10% or less. Last big downhill session 10 to 14 days out. posts.title: Myth vs proof: start everything as early as possible (Backup item, ultra Reel slot)
posts.caption:
Myth: start everything as early as possible.

Proof: each adaptation builds and fades at its own speed. Heat gains fade by about 2.5% for every day without heat, so a heat block months out is mostly gone by race day. In an older study, one downhill session protected the legs for up to about 6 weeks, and the effect was gone at 9. Climbing strength, on the other hand, lasts well.

When to start, counted back from race day:

✅ Heat: build 6 to 2 weeks out, then 1 to 2 short sessions a week to keep it
✅ Downhill: build from 12 to 8 weeks out, biggest weeks 5 to 3 weeks out, last big session 10 to 14 days before
✅ Gut: start 12 to 8 weeks out, race-level carbs by 4 to 6 weeks out, then race fuel in every long session
✅ Climbing: all block long

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions.

Share this with a training partner who starts everything in week 1.

SOURCES: Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows. Heat fade: Daanen et al. 2018, Sports Medicine. Downhill protection: Byrnes et al. 1985.

#raceproof #raceprep #heattraining #downhillrunning #marathontraining

posts.title: Research blog: Does a sauna after running help? (article 5)
posts.caption:
Does a sauna after running help? Probably a little. In 6 runners, 3 weeks of sauna after training let them run 32% longer to exhaustion, which the authors estimate is worth about 1.9% in a time trial. Small, not 32%.

The likely reason is more blood: plasma volume rose 7.1%. Hot baths after runs look similar. In 17 men, 6 days of 104°F (40°C) baths made a 3.1 mi (5 km) time trial in 91°F (33°C) heat 4.9% faster, with no change at 64°F (18°C).

Limits: tiny trials, almost all men. The 1.9% is the authors' estimate, not a measured result, and no one has tested how long sauna gains last.

Our take, not a finding of the studies: optional, counts as heat time for a hot race, and build up slowly.

When to start, counted back from race day:

✅ Heat: 6 to 2 weeks out, building over 10 to 14 days, then some heat to race day. A sauna or hot bath after training counts.

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, high or low blood pressure or its medication, pregnancy, or ever fainted or had heat illness? Talk to your doctor before a sauna or hot baths. Everyone else: after training only, well hydrated, never alone, never after alcohol.

Full article: raceproof.ai/blog/sauna-after-running (link in bio).

SOURCES: Scoon et al. 2007, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. Stanley et al. 2015, European Journal of Applied Physiology. Zurawlew et al. 2016, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. Window: Raceproof adaptation windows.

altText: Research blog, heat. Does a sauna after running help? Probably a little. Not 32%. Scoon et al. 2007, Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 6 runners. From the Raceproof blog: Does a sauna after running help?

The trial: 6 runners, two 3-week blocks. A humid sauna at 194°F (90°C) for about 31 minutes straight after training, 12.7 sessions on average, compared with 3 weeks of normal training without it. Same runners, a 3-week break between. Crossover trial.

The headline number: 32% sounds huge. In a time trial, about 1.9%. Bars: run to exhaustion at 5K race pace +32%; time trial, the authors' estimate +1.9%. A run to exhaustion stretches small changes. The 1.9% is an estimate, not measured. Range 1.3 to 2.4%.

Why it could help: more blood plasma. Plus 7.1% plasma volume in Scoon's 6 runners after the sauna block. In 7 cyclists, plasma volume peaked after 4 sauna sessions, plus 17.8%, no control group, no performance test. Scoon et al. 2007, Stanley et al. 2015.

Hot baths too: 6 days of hot baths after runs. 17 men: 10 sat in 104°F (40°C) water for 40 minutes after each run, 7 in 93°F (34°C). The hot-bath group's 3.1 mi (5 km) time trial: in 91°F (33°C) heat, 4.9% faster; in 64°F (18°C), no change. Zurawlew et al. 2016, randomized controlled trial.

Not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have a heart condition, high or low blood pressure or its medication, pregnancy, or have ever fainted or had heat illness. Everyone else: after training only, well hydrated, never alone, never after alcohol.

Our take, not a finding of the studies: optional, counts as heat time, build up slowly. Expect a small gain, not 32%. For a hot race, Raceproof counts a sauna or hot bath after training as heat time, but never requires it. Heat window 6 to 2 weeks out, then keep some heat. General guidelines, not a prescription. Full article on raceproof.ai.

posts.title: Race breakdown: IRONMAN 70.3 Oceanside (carousel)
posts.caption:
IRONMAN 70.3 Oceanside is on Apr 3, 2027, and terrain on the bike is the pillar to watch. The steepest pitch climbs about 194 ft (59 m) in under 0.31 mi (0.5 km), and the longest climb takes you up to the course's high point before the drops back toward the coast.

The course: 70.3 mi (113.1 km) with about 2,995 ft (913 m) of gain and the same loss, most of the climbing on the bike. The run is two flat loops on the Strand. Typical high 69°F (20.6°C), water 61°F (16.1°C), so heat is low on the list and this is a cool, wetsuit-legal swim. Race day is 19 weeks out.

When to start, counted back from Apr 3:

✅ Bike climbing: key rides with the course's climbing, about 47 ft per mile (9 m per km), all block long from Dec 12
✅ Open water: from Dec 12, then 2 to 4 swims a week from Feb 6, in your race wetsuit
✅ Gut: start between Jan 9 and Feb 6, race-level carbs by Feb 20 to Mar 6
✅ Pacing: race power and pace in long rides and bricks from Jan 23
✅ Taper: the final 2 weeks, from Mar 20

General guidelines, not a prescription. The climbing targets come from coaches, not studies.

Full breakdown: raceproof.ai/races/ironman-70-3-oceanside (link in bio).

SOURCES: Race numbers: Raceproof's IRONMAN 70.3 Oceanside race page. Course profile: IRONMAN's official routes. Bike climbing: Kleanthous, 220 Triathlon 2022 (coaching practice). Open water: Hayes, 220 Triathlon 2026. Wetsuit rule: Raceproof adaptation rates. Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows.

posts.title: Education: Pacing, turkey trot as a pacing test
posts.caption:
Running a turkey trot next week? Use it as a pacing test.

In 78,912 Boston Marathon finishers, 26.6% of those who started more than 5% faster than their average pace hit the wall. Of those who started near their average pace, 1.5% did. A short race is a cheap place to see what your first mile does when the gun goes off.

The test: pick the pace you could hold for the whole race, run mile 1 at it, then compare mile 1 with your average. More than 5% faster means you went out too fast. Not far slower either: in a review of pacing studies, long slow starts were linked to worse results.

When to start, counted back from your goal race:

✅ Pacing: goal-pace work in long runs from 10 weeks out, last long goal-pace run about 4 weeks out

General guidelines, not a prescription. The 5% line comes from a marathon study (observational, Boston qualifiers on one net-downhill course), and the amounts of goal-pace work come from coaches, not studies.

Save this for your next build.

SOURCES: Dong & Li 2026, PLOS ONE. Deaner et al. 2015, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. Ramos-Campo et al. 2026, Sports Medicine. Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows and adaptation rates (coaching practice: McMillan, summarizing Pfitzinger).

#raceproof #marathontraining #marathonrunner #raceprep #runningcommunity
altText: Education, pacing. Turkey trot? Use it as a pacing test. A short race shows what your first mile does when the gun goes off. Raceproof checks: Pacing.

Why the start matters: who hit the wall, by how they started. Started more than 5% faster than their average pace, 26.6%. Started near their average pace, 1.5%. A link, not proof. Boston qualifiers on one net-downhill course. Dong & Li 2026, PLOS ONE, 78,912 Boston finishers, 2015 to 2017.

Most runners slow late. Second half vs first half of a marathon: men slowed 15.6% on average, women 11.7%. Slower finishers slowed more. Deaner et al. 2015, 91,929 results in 14 US marathons, observational.

The test, one race, one number to check. 1, pick the pace you could hold for the whole race. 2, run mile 1 at it, not at the crowd's pace. 3, afterward, compare mile 1 with your average pace. 4, more than 5% faster? You went out too fast. The 5% line comes from the marathon study.

When it counts: the real pacing work starts 10 weeks out. Timeline: goal-pace work in long runs 10 to 1 weeks out, last long goal-pace run about 4 weeks out. Racing in mid April? That's from early February. A turkey trot is early practice. General guidelines, not a prescription. Amounts from coaches, not studies.

A turkey trot is practice. Your long runs are the proof. Readiness row: Pacing, 3 goal-pace long runs done, Ready. Raceproof counts Pacing as proven after 2 or more long runs with the goal-pace block held to the end without fading. Raceproof checks: Pacing. Save this for your next build.

The calendar's 'goal-pace work counts from 10 weeks out' is the Pacing window; 'mid April, from early February' is my example count (Apr 18 minus 10 weeks = Feb 7).
